preamble: Fortition (hardening) of the voiceless velar fricative [x] to the voiceless velar stop [k] is a documented shift. It frequently occurs as a result of language contact—when a language lacking the fricative phoneme adapts loanwords—or as part of a broader fortition process in specific phonetic environments. In Samic, Proto-Uralic *x became *k before vowels (*suxe- 'to row' > Proto-Samic *sukëtēk), while Finnic lost it.

examples.note: Perso-Arabic loanwords with [x] are often adapted as the aspirated stop [kʰ] by speakers who lack [x] in their native inventory.
Occasional fortition in specific dialectal developments from Proto-Germanic.

examples.to: Proto-Samic *sukëtēk > Northern Sami suhkat, Skolt Sami suukkâd
examples.note: Reconstructed stage: the Proto-Uralic velar spirant *x became the stop *k before a vowel; Finnic instead lost it with compensatory lengthening.

examples.to: Proto-Samic *jukëtēk > Northern Sami juhkat, Inari Sami juuḥâđ
examples.note: Reconstructed stage; contrast Proto-Finnic *joodak (Finnish juoda), where *x was lost.

examples.to: Proto-Samic *tuokëtēk 'to sell' > South Sami doekedh, Ume Sami duahkat
examples.note: Reconstructed stage; contrast Proto-Finnic *toodak (Finnish tuoda 'to bring').

examples.to: Proto-Samic *vikëtēk > Skolt Sami viikkâd, Kildin Sami выгкэ

sources: Sammallahti, P. (1998). The Saami Languages: An Introduction. Davvi Girji. https://lccn.loc.gov/00308815
